findings.claim: The workflow header (lines 18–20) states the post-tag observer 'opens a `release-gate-violation` issue for triage' in unqualified present tense, contradicting VERSIONING.md and DISPATCH-NOTE which both correctly qualify the same claim with '(per TF-020H3rg-003)'. The auto-issue step is not implemented in the workflow — no `gh issue create` or equivalent step exists. The fix-round-1 closure of CRIT-SAFE-001 added the two-mode framing to the header but introduced this inaccuracy in doing so.
findings.evidence: release-gate.yml lines 18–20: 'This trigger therefore acts as a LAST-LINE-OF-DEFENSE observer: it annotates the bad tag with SCP-EREL-001 ::error:: and opens a `release-gate-violation` issue for triage.' — unqualified, no TF reference. VERSIONING.md line 147: 'it annotates the bad tag with `SCP-EREL-001` and (per TF-020H3rg-003) opens a `release-gate-violation` issue for triage.' — correctly parenthetically qualified. DISPATCH-NOTE.md lines 109–112: 'The workflow annotates the bad tag with `SCP-EREL-001` and (per TF-020H3rg-003) will open a `release-gate-violation` issue.' — correctly future-tense + qualified. No `gh issue create` step exists anywhere in release-gate.yml. TF-020H3rg-003 in STATUS.md line 118 explicitly marks this as a forward-compat item, not yet implemented.
findings.impact: An operator reading the workflow file's own header to understand post-tag-push behavior will expect a GitHub issue to be created automatically. When no issue appears after a failed push:tags run, they may believe the gate misfired or is misconfigured, wasting debugging time. This divergence directly undermines the two-mode architectural reframing that was the CRIT-SAFE-001 fix-round-1 closure — the workflow header is the primary in-file operational reference and it misrepresents current behavior. VERSIONING.md and DISPATCH-NOTE are consistent with each other; the workflow header is the outlier.
findings.mitigation: Amend release-gate.yml lines 19–20 to match VERSIONING.md's qualified language: change 'and opens a `release-gate-violation` issue for triage' to 'and (per TF-020H3rg-003, not yet implemented) will open a `release-gate-violation` issue for triage'. This makes all three authoritative documents consistent.

findings.claim: The `surface_id` field description in schemas/deprecations.schema.json (lines 26–27) provides surface-kind-specific guidance for all five original enum values (rule, workflow_input, schema_field, annotation_title, branch_protection_helper_flag) but omits equivalent guidance for the newly-added `tag_protection_pattern`. The R1 COR-MAJ-002 mitigation text explicitly called for adding this guidance bullet ('For repository_ruleset: the pattern string, e.g. v* or renovate/v*') but it was not applied in fix-round-1.
findings.evidence: schemas/deprecations.schema.json lines 26–27: 'Identifier of the surface being deprecated. For surface_kind=rule: SCP-R-NNN. For workflow_input: input name (e.g. 'rule-set'). For schema_field: dotted path (e.g. 'policy-check-summary.findings[].rule_id'). For annotation_title: SCP-EXXX. For branch_protection_helper_flag: --flag-name.' — five guidance bullets, no entry for tag_protection_pattern. R1 finding COR-MAJ-002 mitigation (review-correctness.json): 'Add a corresponding surface_id guidance bullet: For repository_ruleset: the pattern string, e.g. v* or renovate/v*.' The schema description line 21–22 was updated (adding tag_protection_pattern description) but the surface_id description was not.
findings.impact: An operator creating the first `tag_protection_pattern` deprecation entry must infer the appropriate surface_id value from VERSIONING.md context (e.g., 'v*' or 'renovate/v*') rather than reading the schema's self-documentation. Incomplete schema-as-documentation relative to the claimed coverage.
findings.mitigation: Append to schemas/deprecations.schema.json surface_id description: 'For tag_protection_pattern: the ruleset pattern string, e.g. v* or renovate/v*.' This closes the gap that the R1 mitigation text identified but fix-round-1 did not apply.

findings.claim: The VERSIONING.md 'Bad-tag recovery procedure' emergency path (lines 197–203) provides the `gh api -X DELETE` command to disable the tag-protection ruleset but omits: (a) the command to discover the numeric ruleset ID required by that command, and (b) the tag-deletion command to run after the ruleset is disabled. An operator following this procedure step-by-step during an actual emergency must independently determine both, extending the window during which tag-protection is disabled.
findings.evidence: VERSIONING.md lines 199–202: '`gh api -X DELETE repos/jrnb2024/standards-control-plane/rulesets/<id>` (requires `administration:write` PAT); delete the bad tag; restore the ruleset.' The `<id>` placeholder is undefined. The phrase 'delete the bad tag' has no associated shell command. The phrase 'restore the ruleset' has no associated command or pointer to the idempotent restore script. WP-SCP-022 §4.3 specifies that the bad-tag recovery procedure should be operationally complete. The non-emergency path (cut corrected v<X>.<Y+1>.0) is adequately described; the emergency-only path is not.
findings.impact: In a real emergency where a security vulnerability was introduced via a bad tag, the operator must spend additional time discovering the ruleset ID and tag-deletion syntax while the protection is disabled. The ruleset-lookup command is non-obvious (`gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets | jq` pattern); the tag-deletion command requires knowing the git ref-deletion API syntax. Emergency procedures must be copy-pasteable to minimize protection-gap window.
findings.mitigation: Add to the emergency path in VERSIONING.md: (1) Ruleset ID lookup: `gh api repos/jrnb2024/standards-control-plane/rulesets | python3 -c 'import json,sys; [print(r["id"], r["name"]) for r in json.load(sys.stdin)]'` (2) Tag deletion after ruleset removed: `git push --delete origin <bad-tag>` (3) Ruleset restore: `bash scripts/configure-020j-protections.sh` (idempotent per D-030).

findings.claim: The tampering-warning check at release-gate.yml line 211 (`if ann_major < cand_major - 1`) and the structural-inconsistency violation at lines 237–243 (`else` branch) can co-fire for the same deprecation entry when `target == candidate` AND `ann_major < cand_major - 1`. This emits both `::warning::SCP-EREL-001-warn` and `::error::SCP-EREL-001` for a single entry. The warning's language ('verify this is not a backdated entry') implies operator verification can unblock the gate, while the structural-inconsistency error unconditionally refuses.
findings.evidence: release-gate.yml lines 211–215: `if ann_major < cand_major - 1:` fires for any entry (target-matched or not) where announced is 2+ majors behind. release-gate.yml line 218: `if target != candidate: continue` — for target-matched entries this continue is NOT taken. release-gate.yml lines 232–243: the `else` branch fires when `target == candidate` AND `ann_major != cand_major` AND `ann_major != cand_major - 1`, i.e., exactly when `ann_major < cand_major - 1` and target matches. Both warning (non-blocking, line 246) and error (blocking, line 249) are appended and printed. Example: candidate=v3.0.0, entry target=v3.0.0, announced=v1.0.0 → tampering warning fires (1 < 2) then structural-inconsistency error fires (1 ≠ 2 and 1 ≠ 1). Gate correctly refuses (sys.exit(1) line 255).
findings.impact: No correctness impact — the hard refusal is unconditional and correct. Operator UX concern only: during debugging the operator sees two annotations for one entry with apparently contradictory imperatives ('verify this' vs hard refusal). This edge case is rare (two-major gap with same-candidate target is an unusual deprecation shape) but confusing when it occurs.
